subject: Culture
title: Politeness Systems
description: A quick, practical guide to Politeness Systems.

hook.text: Japanese has seven levels of formality. Using the wrong one with your boss can end a career.

buildup.text: Korean similarly requires speakers to mark social rank in every sentence through verb endings.

discovery.text: English flattened its hierarchy when 'thou' disappeared. We lost the ability to encode rank grammatically.

twist.text: French 'tu' vs 'vous' still trips up tourists. Using 'tu' with a stranger is either intimate or insulting.

climax.text: In cultures with steep politeness systems, saying exactly the same words in the wrong register is the insult.

punchline.text: Some languages make you choose your rank with every verb.

quiz.question: Which English pronoun was lost, removing a built-in formality distinction?

details.summary: Languages encode social hierarchy through politeness systems — Japanese has multiple formality levels requiring different verb forms based on the listener's social status. Korean has seven speech levels. French distinguishes tu (informal) and vous (formal).
details.whyItMatters: Politeness systems reveal how languages enforce social hierarchies. Speaking incorrectly to a superior is not just rude — it violates the social order embedded in the language itself.
takeaways: Japanese keigo (honorific language) has three distinct levels
Korean has seven speech levels reflecting social relationships
Using the wrong politeness level can be deeply offensive

faq.question: How does Japanese politeness work?
faq.answer: Japanese keigo has three main levels: sonkeigo (respectful language elevating the listener), kenjougo (humble language lowering the speaker), and teineigo (polite neutral language). Each carries different verb forms, vocabulary, and even sentence structures.

faq.question: Why do some languages have more politeness levels than others?
faq.answer: Languages with elaborate politeness systems tend to develop in hierarchical societies where social relationships are precisely stratified. Korean's seven speech levels reflect Confucian hierarchy. Japanese keigo reflects feudal social organization.
